# Why apps {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Notebooks explore; apps deliver

A notebook is **for you**: messy, sequential, requires Python.

An app is **for them**: a stakeholder, a grader, the public — people who will *never* run your cells.

| | Notebook | Streamlit app |
|---|---|---|
| Audience | you | others |
| Interaction | edit & re-run | widgets |
| Requires | Python env | a URL |
| Question style | fixed | *their* question |

## Streamlit's bet: an app is just a script

```python
import streamlit as st
import plotly.express as px

st.title("Tips Explorer")
df = px.data.tips()
day = st.selectbox("Day", sorted(df["day"].unique()))
st.scatter_chart(df[df["day"] == day], x="total_bill", y="tip")
```

No HTML, no JavaScript, no callbacks. The price of that simplicity is one unusual idea — the execution model.

# The re-run model {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## The whole script re-runs on every interaction

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mp
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 3.4))
boxes = [("user moves\na widget", "#EAF2F6"), ("ENTIRE script\nre-runs top→bottom", "#2E6E8E"),
         ("new outputs\nrendered", "#EAF2F6")]
for i, (txt, col) in enumerate(boxes):
    fc = col; tc = "white" if col == "#2E6E8E" else "#1a1a1a"
    ax.add_patch(mp.FancyBboxPatch((i*3.3, 0.5), 2.6, 1.6, boxstyle="round,pad=0.1", fc=fc, ec="#2E6E8E"))
    ax.text(i*3.3+1.3, 1.3, txt, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=11, color=tc)
    if i < 2:
        ax.annotate("", xy=(i*3.3+3.1, 1.3), xytext=(i*3.3+2.8, 1.3),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=2, color="#5a6672"))
ax.annotate("", xy=(1.3, 0.45), xytext=(7.9, 0.45),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=1.5, color="#d9534f",
                            connectionstyle="arc3,rad=0.25"))
ax.text(4.6, -0.45, "…and again on the next interaction", ha="center", fontsize=10, color="#d9534f")
ax.set_xlim(-0.4, 10.3); ax.set_ylim(-0.8, 2.6); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Three consequences: it's why the code stays simple, why **plain variables reset** every interaction, and why **slow code becomes unbearable**.

## Consequence 1: state needs `session_state`

```python
count = 0                      # ← resets to 0 on EVERY re-run: useless
if st.button("Click"): count += 1   # forever prints 1

if "count" not in st.session_state:  # ← survives re-runs
    st.session_state.count = 0
if st.button("Click"):
    st.session_state.count += 1
```

Rule of thumb: anything that must **survive an interaction** lives in `st.session_state`.

## Consequence 2: slow code needs caching

```python
@st.cache_data            # cache key = the function's arguments
def load_data(path):
    return pd.read_csv(path)        # runs ONCE per unique path

df = load_data("big.csv")           # instant on every later re-run
```

- `@st.cache_data` — dataframes, results, anything copyable
- `@st.cache_resource` — models, DB connections (shared, not copied)

In Block 2 you'll *feel* the difference: a 3-second load, with and without.

# Layout & deployment {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Layout vocabulary {.smaller}

- `st.sidebar` — controls live here; content stays clean
- `st.columns(n)` — metrics and side-by-side charts
- `st.tabs([...])` — alternate views without scrolling
- `st.metric` — the big-number-with-delta pattern dashboards love

::: {.gw-box}
Design principle from Week 2 still rules: the *reader's* main comparison gets the best real estate, controls get the sidebar.
:::

## Deployment: from laptop to URL

1. Push `app.py` + `requirements.txt` to a **GitHub repo**
2. share.streamlit.io → **New app** → pick the repo
3. Share the URL

That's Streamlit Community Cloud (free). Caveats worth knowing: apps **sleep** when idle, resources are modest, and secrets go in app settings — never in the repo. (Weeks 12–14: the same idea for your model server.)
